text:
Recent research separates semantic similarity from useful product relationships. The [TREC recommendation task](https://trec-product-search.github.io/recommendations.html) explicitly distinguishes substitutes and complements; a [2024 survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16135) further highlights asymmetric complementarity and relationships where substitution and complementarity coexist. Neither lexical overlap nor co-occurrence alone establishes functional compatibility. [HNLMRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04726) finds semantic hard-negative sampling promising but vulnerable to noisy samples and insufficient behavioral constraints. Unobserved candidates therefore should not automatically receive negative preference labels.

For diagnostics, adapt the established [contrast-set approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.02709): construct closely matched candidate pairs with small, explicitly documented differences that change suitability under a stated requirement. Using available titles/descriptions, potential contrasts include connector compatibility, dimensions, device generation, tool function, movie edition/content, or album versus accessory. These are proposed probes, not established labels: require supporting text for both candidates, distinguish incompatibility from mere difference, and avoid interpreting interaction history as proof of current ownership or intent. Measure pairwise ranking accuracy and score margins against a lexical-similarity baseline; stratify by category and contrast type.

Report metadata coverage and the fraction of pairs with sufficient evidence alongside diagnostic accuracy. Abstain when compatibility, intended function, or the user requirement cannot be established. Broader [2026 evidence-sufficiency research](https://doi.org/10.32604/cmc.2026.086343) supports evaluating partially supported, absent, and conflicting evidence separately, although it concerns RAG rather than recommendation. Such probes diagnose sensitivity to explicit constraints; they do not establish user dislike, next-purchase utility, or improved benchmark HR@10.
